tiles.title: Login
tiles.opener: Who uses it: every user, before anything else — the first screen and, for anyone who forgets a password, a recurring one. What "done" looks like: signed in, or told exactly why not without leaking which part was wrong. The one screen every ERP app has and the one where getting the details wrong locks real users out. Composed entirely from existing components, zero new CSS: .bo-widget (the card primitive) centers the form on the canvas, fields are plain .bo-form-fields with the correct autocomplete tokens (username / current-password — this is what lets password managers fill the form), and errors use the same validation-summary pattern as any other form. Try it: submit the empty form. Not for re-authentication mid-task — when a workspace needs a step-up credential check without abandoning the screen the user was on (confirming a destructive action, re-entering a password after a session timeout), a full-page navigation throws away that context; use a dialog carrying the same two fields instead. This page is for the one navigation every session starts with, not an interruption inside one.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: every user, before anything else — the first screen and, for anyone who forgets a password, a recurring one.…

tiles.title: Error pages
tiles.opener: Who uses it: every user, eventually — a stale bookmark, a link shared before a record moved, a permission that changed since yesterday, a request that failed server-side. How often: rare per user, universal per app — every ERP hits all three of 404, 403 and 500 sooner or later. What "done" looks like: the reader is never at a dead end — one clear sentence for what happened, and at least one real place to go next. Three status codes, ONE shape: icon, title, description, actions — .bo-state and .bo-state--error, already shipped, nothing new. Not for a section failing to load inside a page you're still on — a table or panel that can't fetch its own data is .bo-state--error used inline, right where the section was, with the rest of the screen still usable. This pattern is for when the NAVIGATION itself failed, not one region of a page that otherwise worked.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: every user, eventually — a stale bookmark, a link shared before a record moved, a permission that changed since yesterday,…

tiles.title: App launch
tiles.opener: Who uses it: anyone opening the suite, every session — the first screen after sign-in. What "done" looks like: the right app is one tap away, whether it's a favourite or three deep in a category. A suite entry screen — the icon-grid launcher (the "Bento UI" / tablet-launcher archetype from the device-coverage table — same .bo-widget-grid container-query mechanism as a dashboard, at a smaller tile size, not a new grid component). Tiles are plain links composed into .bo-widget cards with real CSS icons (themable currentColor glyphs) where a glyph is genuinely right, an initials chip where none is, and inline <svg> where a tenant brings their own; the category row is the ordinary tabs pattern; a "folder" tile is just a widget whose body holds a cluster of small tiles. Zero new CSS. Not for returning a user to a specific record they already know — a bookmark, a notification, or a saved link should land directly on the object page or the list report, never route back through the launcher grid to get there.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: anyone opening the suite, every session — the first screen after sign-in.…

tiles.title: Command bar
tiles.opener: Who uses it: power users who know what they want — a dispatcher jumping to PO-88213, a controller running "post period" — without walking the menu. How often: dozens of times a day, which is why it is keyboard-first and why the shortcut must never be stolen from the browser. What "done" looks like: they typed a few characters and the screen they wanted is open, hands never leaving the keyboard. Not a replacement for navigation — it rewards people who already know the name of the thing. A first-time or occasional user needs the visible structure of app launch, and a user narrowing an unknown set needs the filter panel; a command bar answers neither.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: power users who know what they want — a dispatcher jumping to PO-88213, a controller running "post period" — without…

tiles.title: Role home
tiles.opener: Who uses it: every named role — a buyer, an approver, a warehouse supervisor — each seeing their own version. How often: the first screen after sign-in, and the one they come back to between tasks. What "done" looks like: the reader knows in one glance whether anything needs them, and leaves for the screen that resolves it. Not a launcher — a tile grid of every app someone could open is app launch; this shows live content about their work. And not a dashboard: the reporting dashboard monitors the business (is the period on track), a role home monitors my work (is anything waiting on me). Same widgets, different subject — and confusing the two is how a home screen turns into a chart wall nobody acts on.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: every named role — a buyer, an approver, a warehouse supervisor — each seeing their own version.…

tiles.title: List report
tiles.opener: Who uses it: AP clerks, all day — the screen they live in. What "done" looks like: find the invoices that need action, act on them in bulk, and never lose your place. Composed entirely from shipped components; the data table page documents the table itself, this page documents the screen. Not for a single record's full detail — once a clerk opens one invoice to review or act on it alone, that screen is a record detail (or an object page for a richer one); list-report's job stops at finding and bulk-acting on rows, not deep-diving into one.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: AP clerks, all day — the screen they live in.…

tiles.title: Advanced filter panel
tiles.opener: The filter set that outgrew the bar. A finance or purchasing user opens the same list a dozen times a day and narrows it a different way each time — cost centre, status, date range, amount band. They do not want twelve controls permanently across the top; they want the two they use constantly visible and the rest a click away. "Done" means the list reloads and what is currently filtering it stays visible after the panel closes — a filter you cannot see is a filter you will forget you set, and then mistrust the numbers. Not for a list with one obvious narrowing dimension — a single search box or a two-option status filter is already inline in the list report's own bar; reach for the grouped, chip-backed panel here only once distinct facets pile up (cost centre, date band, status, and more), not by default for every list.
tiles.openerShort: The filter set that outgrew the bar.…

tiles.title: Value help
tiles.opener: Who uses it: anyone typing a code they cannot remember — a buyer picking a material out of forty thousand, a clerk choosing a cost centre; dozens of times a day, inside a form they are part-way through. What "done" looks like: the right code is in the field, and the reader is back where they were with nothing else lost. The picker is a detour, not a destination — which is why choosing must put focus back in the field they were filling, not leave it at the top of the document. Not when the option set is small — a couple dozen fixed choices belong in a plain native select, not a dialog with search and paging behind it. This pattern is for the case a select cannot handle: a list too large to enumerate in one control.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: anyone typing a code they cannot remember — a buyer picking a material out of forty thousand, a clerk choosing a cost…

tiles.title: Record detail
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever owns this record, checking its status or adding to its history — a buyer, an approver, anyone who clicked in from a list row. How often: every time a list row is opened — this is the default landing for "tell me about this one," many times a day across a team. What "done" looks like: the current state is read in one glance, without opening anything else. The composed detail screen behind any list row: record cards, a status timeline, and an audit trail stacked in a feed — all standard components, generic to any ERP. This example is a purchase order; the shape is the same for an invoice, a change request, or a leave request. Not once the record stops fitting in one scan — when a reader has to hunt for a section, it wants anchor navigation and a sticky action bar, which is object page. Same content, different reading problem.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: whoever owns this record, checking its status or adding to its history — a buyer, an approver, anyone who clicked in from a…

tiles.title: Master-detail
tiles.opener: M2 of the four data-maintenance patterns (and the most common one in practice): a list of records, and clicking a row opens that record's fields in a panel beside the list or a dialog over it. A back-office user uses this all day — find the vendor, fix two fields, move on — and "done" means the list stays put, keeping their scroll position, filters and sort, while only the detail changes. Not when one record deserves the whole screen — the split exists so a user can move ALONG the list without losing their place; if they are working one record end to end, the panel is just a narrower object page.
tiles.openerShort: M2 of the four data-maintenance patterns (and the most common one in practice): a list of records, and clicking a row opens that…

tiles.title: Multi-column detail form
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever owns the record — a buyer editing a PO, an admin fixing vendor details; occasional, high-stakes edits where losing work is unacceptable. What "done" looks like: every change saved (or explicitly discarded) with no silent loss. The edit-screen counterpart to record detail: a full purchase-order edit form, composed entirely from existing components — .bo-form-section fieldsets, the .bo-form-row auto-fit column grid, the line-items data table, and a sticky .bo-form-actions bar. Nothing new to learn; .bo-form-row already collapses to one column on narrow screens by construction (auto-fit, not a fixed column count) — resize the window to see it. Not for reading a record — a form styles fields for ENTRY, and rendering read-only values as inputs tells the user they can change things they cannot. Read surfaces are record detail and object page.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: whoever owns the record — a buyer editing a PO, an admin fixing vendor details; occasional, high-stakes edits where losing…

tiles.title: Object page
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever owns one record end to end — a buyer opening a PO, an approver checking it before signing; many times a day, one object at a time. What "done" looks like: the reader can see the object's status without scrolling, reach any section in one click, and act on it from anywhere on the page. The long-record counterpart to record detail: same content, but too tall to take in at once, so it gains navigation of its own. Not for a record you can take in at one glance — the anchor rail and sticky action bar are overhead you only earn by being long. That one is record detail.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: whoever owns one record end to end — a buyer opening a PO, an approver checking it before signing; many times a day, one…

tiles.title: Validation summary
tiles.opener: Who uses it: anyone filling a form with more than a couple of required fields — worth it the moment a reader could miss which field failed. What "done" looks like: every problem named in one place AND on its field, with nothing to hunt for. On submit, if the form is invalid: list every problem field up top, move focus to that summary first (not straight into a field — a screen-reader user hears the overview before jumping in), and let each link focus its exact field. Composed entirely from existing components — the summary box is just .bo-alert bo-alert--danger, and every field's error state (red border, red label, required asterisk) comes free from the existing :user-invalid styling already in .bo-form-field. Try it: submit the empty form below. Not for per-row saves — in an editable grid each row saves on its own (PATCH per line, 422 → that row re-rendered with cell errors), so a failure comes back on the row the user just acted on and a summary would only restate it. The summary earns its place on a document-level submit — posting the whole form — where several fields can fail at once, including some scrolled out of view.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: anyone filling a form with more than a couple of required fields — worth it the moment a reader could miss which field failed.…

tiles.title: Multi-step wizard
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever is creating something too long for one screen, guided rather than dropped into a form — most often a first-time or occasional flow. What "done" looks like: every step completed or explicitly skippable, submitted once, and resumable if abandoned partway. A real multi-step flow — one panel visible at a time, Back/Next move between them — as opposed to detail form's multi-section single screen. Composed from the existing .bo-stepper progress indicator plus a new opt-in behavior, initWizard(), that keeps the stepper and the visible panel in sync and moves focus to each new panel — the panels themselves are plain .bo-form-section fieldsets, nothing new to learn there. Not for a routine single-step task — if there is nothing to walk someone through, a wizard's Back/Next scaffolding is friction with no payoff; use a plain detail form instead. Its Next/Submit pair is the one legitimate two-primary-action layout in this system precisely because it exists to gate a guided multi-step flow, not a single screen.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: whoever is creating something too long for one screen, guided rather than dropped into a form — most often a first-time or…

tiles.title: Staging / batch result
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever maintains data in bulk — an uploaded file, an interface run, a mass posting. How often: month-end and whenever a supplier sends a spreadsheet. What "done" looks like: every submitted row either became a record or is still on screen saying why it didn't. This is the landing place that makes the bulk action contract work for data the user has not seen yet. Not for a handful of records — three or four rows do not need a validate/apply split with per-row verdicts; edit them one at a time in a plain detail form. This pattern earns its complexity only once the count is large enough that a human cannot eyeball every row before committing.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: whoever maintains data in bulk — an uploaded file, an interface run, a mass posting.…

tiles.title: Editable grid
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever enters or corrects line items — a buyer building a PO, a warehouse clerk keying a pick list. What "done" looks like: every row either saved or still marked unsaved, never silently dropped. Line-item entry — a PO, an invoice, a pick list — composed entirely from existing pieces, presented as a graded path. Simple: plain text/number cells with dirty-state + Save/Cancel — that's the data-table page's multi-row inline edit, start there. Medium (first demo below): a combobox lookup cell, cell-level validation, add/remove lines. Money & unit cells: currency and unit as real separate fields inside a row. Advanced: every cell type, realtime totals, and the save-per-change mode. The full picture: a composite PO line-items editor putting all of it in one table. Not for a table that's read far more often than edited — a plain data table costs nothing and doesn't ship Save/Cancel machinery nobody triggers. Zero new CSS at every step — the grid is the same primitives, composed harder.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: whoever enters or corrects line items — a buyer building a PO, a warehouse clerk keying a pick list.…

tiles.title: Inbox
tiles.opener: Who uses it: every ERP user, first thing — the screen a working day starts on. How often: continuously; it is the tab that stays open. What "done" looks like: the list is empty of things that need you — every row either acted on or explicitly handed off. An inbox is cross-type and cross-process: approvals, exceptions, assigned tasks and failed jobs in ONE list, and every row says why it is yours. Not for one document type's approval queue — that scoped, single-process view is the approval workflow's job; and not a feed of things that merely happened — that is notification's contract. The inbox holds only rows that block on a person.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: every ERP user, first thing — the screen a working day starts on. How often: continuously; it is the tab that stays open.…

tiles.title: Approval workflow
tiles.opener: Who uses it: an approver named in the chain — a manager, a cost-centre owner, finance. How often: whenever a document reaches their step, which for most approvers is a handful of times a week. What "done" looks like: the decision recorded, the next person notified, nothing silently stuck. The composed slice-3 screen: wizard stepper, status timeline, approval queue (the data-table pattern you already know), and the audit trail. State always has two channels: a visible non-color cue (the glyph) and programmatic state (visually-hidden text / aria-current) — one without the other is a defect. Not for a record with no decision to make — a plain edit to a record's own fields, with nobody else's sign-off in the way, is record-detail's job; reach for this pattern only when a chain of people, not just the owner, has to act before the record can move.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: an approver named in the chain — a manager, a cost-centre owner, finance.…

tiles.title: Bulk actions
tiles.opener: Who uses it: an AP clerk clearing a queue — select many, act once. What "done" looks like: every selected record either changed or explained why it didn't. The failure mode this pattern exists to prevent is the silent one: an action that reports success while quietly skipping rows. Not for changing one record — a single row's fields belong on the object page or record-detail; this pattern's whole cost (out-of-band summary, per-row reasons, the transient-state rule) only pays for itself once more than one record is changing at once.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: an AP clerk clearing a queue — select many, act once.…

tiles.title: Kanban board
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever needs to see WHERE a batch of things stands, all at once — a production planner watching orders move through stages, a fulfilment lead watching shipments. How often: a screen left open, glanced at through a shift. What "done" looks like: every card in the lane that matches its real state, and moving one is a single deliberate act. Not for finding one specific record — that is list report, grouped by status if stage is what matters; a board earns its place only when the SHAPE of stages side-by-side is the thing being read, not any one row's fields. Not drag-and-drop — moving a card here is a menu action, not a drag gesture; see why below.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: whoever needs to see WHERE a batch of things stands, all at once — a production planner watching orders move through…

tiles.title: Reporting dashboard
tiles.opener: Who uses it: a manager checking whether this period's AP activity is on track and where the exceptions are. What "done" looks like: three numbers read at a glance, an exception spotted without opening a single invoice. Composed entirely from existing components: breadcrumb, filter bar + saved views, a stat-tile row, and a widget grid mixing a data table, an audit-style activity feed, and a collapsible notes card. Zero new CSS — everything here already has its own component page. Not for an actionable worklist — this screen is read-only situational awareness: numbers and a feed a manager scans, not a queue anyone works from. A screen whose whole job is triaging items one by one is an inbox or a job monitor, not this.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: a manager checking whether this period's AP activity is on track and where the exceptions are.…

tiles.title: Report
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever must answer a specific question with numbers — an accountant at close, a buyer checking open commitments. How often: on demand, and on a schedule someone else set. What "done" looks like: the result is on screen, printed, or exported, and the parameters that produced it are visible beside it. A report is run: you choose parameters, it executes, you read the result. Not for monitoring — a screen you leave open to watch the business is the reporting dashboard; this one answers one question, once, with stated inputs. Not a list screen either: list report finds documents to act on, a report produces figures to read.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: whoever must answer a specific question with numbers — an accountant at close, a buyer checking open commitments.…

tiles.title: Output form
tiles.opener: Who uses it: nobody, on screen — this is the artefact the ERP emits: a purchase order sent to a vendor, an invoice, a delivery note travelling with goods. How often: every time a document is issued, usually unattended. What "done" looks like: a page a stranger can read without your system — sender, recipient, document number, lines, totals, terms — that survives pagination and a black-and-white printer. Not a screen, and not a PDF engine — if a person needs to work with the record, that is the object page; and rendering the actual PDF is your server's job (see the grill verdict below), not this framework's.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: nobody, on screen — this is the artefact the ERP emits: a purchase order sent to a vendor, an invoice, a delivery note…

tiles.title: Notification
tiles.opener: Who uses it: anyone whose work finishes while they are not watching — a posting run, an export, an approval granted upstream. How often: glanced at many times a day, read fully a few. What "done" looks like: the unread count is zero because each item was seen and either dismissed or followed. This is the surface for things that happened; it never blocks on you. Not for work that needs your action — a row that blocks on a person belongs in the inbox, not here; and not for things happening while you watch — that is an alert or toast's moment. The grill that settled the shape (101.5): it is BOTH a navbar glance and a screen — the bell dropdown shows the latest few, the screen holds the readable history — and both compose from shipped pieces.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: anyone whose work finishes while they are not watching — a posting run, an export, an approval granted upstream.…

tiles.title: Job monitor
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever is accountable when unattended work fails — an integrations admin, an ops lead, the person the inbox assigned an exception to. How often: a glance most days, a deep look the moment something is late. What "done" looks like: every scheduled job shows its last result and next run, and nothing has failed silently. Not for authoring schedules — cron expressions, dependency chains and retry policy are your ERP's admin module; this screen is scoped to monitoring jobs someone already scheduled — view, retry, cancel, nothing that changes what runs next time. And not the place to read one run's own numbers: a finished job links to its own result (a report or a staging screen); this page only tracks whether runs happened and how they went.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: whoever is accountable when unattended work fails — an integrations admin, an ops lead, the person the inbox assigned an…

tiles.title: Schedule
tiles.opener: A planner or supervisor scans a month for what is booked — deliveries, maintenance windows, shift cover — several times a day during a busy week, and once a day otherwise. "Done" is picking a day and seeing exactly what is on it without losing the month underneath, the same swap discipline master-detail uses for a list and a record. Not for authoring a schedule — creating, moving or cancelling entries is the admin module's job, not this screen's — and not for one entry's own detail or history, which belongs to record detail, not a month grid. This page only answers "what is on this day".
tiles.openerShort: A planner or supervisor scans a month for what is booked — deliveries, maintenance windows, shift cover — several times a day during a…

tiles.title: Settings & admin
tiles.opener: Who uses it: a workspace admin, occasionally a first-time setup wizard. How often: rarely per person, but every workspace has one. What "done" looks like: a section's values saved, or an unsaved change clearly marked before the admin navigates away. Composed entirely from existing components — .bo-tabs to split General/Users/Notifications, .bo-form-section fieldsets, .bo-checkbox for on/off preferences (there is no separate "switch" component — a labeled checkbox already covers the same setting, per the "one component, many settings" principle), and the data table for the user list. Nothing new to learn. Not for a single end user's own preferences — this screen is workspace-wide configuration an admin changes for everyone (tabs, a member list, org defaults). One person editing their own notification or display preferences needs none of that surface; use a plain detail form scoped to that person instead.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: a workspace admin, occasionally a first-time setup wizard. How often: rarely per person, but every workspace has one.…

tiles.title: RF task menu
tiles.opener: Who uses it: a warehouse floor worker, first screen after signing into the handheld — every RF shift starts here. What "done" looks like: the next task is one tap away, with 3-6 items visible at once, never a menu to search. Not for a general app launcher with dozens of destinations — that's App launch, which this reuses the mechanism from at a different scale: same .bo-widget-grid container-query grid, glove-sized tiles instead of icon tiles, and data-density="spacious" for one-handed, often-gloved use. An RF device runs a handful of tasks per shift, not a suite — this menu stays that short on purpose (roadmap 109.7).
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: a warehouse floor worker, first screen after signing into the handheld — every RF shift starts here.…

tiles.title: RF task queue
tiles.opener: Who uses it: a warehouse floor worker after picking a task from the RF task menu — "what's next" for that task type. What "done" looks like: the worker reads top-to-bottom, taps the top row, and starts working it — no cross-referencing between columns. Not for editing a line's data on this screen — see Editable, refused below. Composed from .bo-data-table at data-density="spacious", two narrow columns — the SAME component and profile membership Goods receipt's own receiving log already proves at 360px (roadmap 59.4); this page is a second, task-queue-shaped use of that same proof, not a new claim about the component.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: a warehouse floor worker after picking a task from the RF task menu — "what's next" for that task type.…

tiles.title: Goods receipt (RF scanner)
tiles.opener: Who uses it: a warehouse floor worker, one-handed and often gloved, holding a scanner instead of a mouse. What "done" looks like: every expected line accounted for — received in full, received partial, or explicitly not received — before the receipt posts. A GR (goods receipt) screen driven by a handheld RF scanner — the scanner types the barcode fast and sends Enter, so the field needs to stay focused and clear itself between scans. Composed from data-scan-input (new opt-in behavior, no new CSS — a plain .bo-input), the existing .bo-quantity at data-density="spacious" for a warehouse-floor large target, and the data table for the receiving log. A visually-hidden aria-live="polite" region (linked via the field's own aria-describedby) announces each successful scan — a screen-reader/low-vision RF user gets non-visual confirmation without it being read for every sighted user. Not for a desk-based receiving clerk keying a paper packing slip. Without a physical scanner there is no barcode to feed the always-focused field, the spacious steppers just waste screen space, and the workflow is really "type these numbers in and check them" — that's a detail form at normal density, not this pattern.
tiles.openerShort: Who uses it: a warehouse floor worker, one-handed and often gloved, holding a scanner instead of a mouse.…
